title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Who Woke the Sleeping Giant
moral: The greatest power is the gentle kind, the kind that opens eyes rather than forces hands.

pages.content:
The plateau was old in the way that mountains are old: not just in years but in layers, each one a different age of the world pressed flat and stacked. {{NAME}} had climbed it for the fossils, which were everywhere in the orange rock, the pressed memories of creatures that had once been enormous and alive and were now beautiful and still.

The plateau was also, it turned out, inhabited. Not by anything large. By something barely visible: a fairy city built between the fossils themselves, tiny spires rising from the eye socket of an ammonite, lantern-lit bridges spanning a crack in the limestone where an ancient fern had turned to stone.

A fairy named Jora found him before he found her, landing on the rim of his copper headband with the confidence of someone claiming a perfectly reasonable perch. She was the colour of amber in sunlight, with wings like hammered gold, and she was regarding the plateau below them with an expression of tremendous, barely contained concern.

'You feel it too,' she said. It was not a question. {{NAME}} had felt it since he crested the ridge: a deep, slow reverberation rising through the rock. Not geological. Rhythmic.

pages.content:
Jora explained quickly, in the clipped way of someone working against a clock that only they can hear. The deep reverberations came from beneath the plateau: a stegosaurus, alive and very much awake after millions of years of dormancy, in the way that extraordinary things sometimes are on extraordinary plateaus. She was not aggressive. She was disoriented, and a disoriented stegosaurus the size of a city bus thrashing underground would do significant damage to the fairy city in about one hour.

{{NAME}}'s expression went through several phases at once: the surprise and absolute belief of someone who has read enough about the world to know it is bigger than he thought, followed by the focused readiness of someone who has decided what he is going to do about it.

'She needs to know where she is,' Jora said, tapping her small fingers together rapidly. 'She needs a voice she can feel. Dinosaurs navigated by sound, we think. By resonance. But the fairy city can't produce a frequency large enough to reach her without tearing itself apart.'

{{NAME}}'s eyebrows went up. 'But a person can.'

pages.content:
Jora led him to the resonance point, a shallow bowl in the plateau's centre where the stone rang like a bell when struck, and where the reverberations from below were strong enough to feel in {{NAME}}'s whole skeleton.

Around the bowl's edge, every fairy in the city had assembled, hundreds of them, sitting with their wings folded and their hands pressed flat to the stone. They were listening. Their collective attention was a tangible thing, focused and still.

'Low, slow, steady,' Jora said, settling on the stone beside {{NAME}}'s knee. 'Like a heartbeat. She knows that sound.'

{{NAME}} lay flat on the warm stone, pressed his whole body to it, and began to hum. Low, resonant, slow. He felt ridiculous for exactly three seconds and then he felt the stone respond, the frequency of the bowl catching his voice and amplifying it downward, into the rock, into the dark where the stegosaurus moved in her confusion.

The reverberations changed. The thrashing rhythm below began to slow, uncertain at first, then slower, then settling into something that matched his voice almost precisely, a great deep counter-hum from forty metres underground.

pages.content:
The stegosaurus rose slowly, the way dawn rises: first a lightening, then a presence, then suddenly, overwhelming and complete. She came up through a fissure on the plateau's far side that the fairies had known about and {{NAME}} had not, and she stood in the amber late-day light like something out of the deepest possible dream.

She was enormous. Her plates caught the sun in every shade of terracotta and rust. Her tail swayed, slow and ponderous. She turned her small, ancient head and found the resonance bowl, found {{NAME}} sitting upright on the stone, and took one step toward him that shook the whole plateau.

Then she lay down. Simply, heavily, completely, like a mountain deciding it had finished standing. The warm stone sighed under her weight.

The fairy city went perfectly silent. Then, from every spire and bridge and lantern-lit window, a sound rose: the fairies were singing, a high, sustained, golden note that the stegosaurus seemed to hear in the same deep place where she had heard {{NAME}}'s humming. Her eyes closed. Her breathing deepened.

{{NAME}} sat beside her enormous head and felt the ground warm and solid and alive beneath him.

pages.content:
As the plateau turned gold and then rose in the last of the light, the stegosaurus slept, her slow deep breathing making the stone hum very faintly in a frequency {{NAME}} could feel more than hear. The fairy city went about its restored business: lights appearing in windows, tiny lanterns being relit on the bridges over the stone fern.

Jora sat on {{NAME}}'s knee and did not speak for a long time, which he suspected was unusual for her. Below the plateau, the world went on, ordinary and unaware.

{{NAME}} lay back on the warm stone with his hands behind his head. The copper headband had slipped sideways and he did not bother to fix it. Above him the plateau's sky was the particular shade of deep blue that comes just before the first stars.

The stegosaurus's next breath washed over him warm and ancient. The fairies' lanterns reflected in the fossils all around.

His eyes grew slow and heavy. Tomorrow, Jora had mentioned, the stegosaurus might want to explore the plateau. And she was going to need a guide.

Goodnight, resonant one. Dream of deep harmonies, and wonder where those footsteps might lead.
